This would make it much easier to verify preprocessor behavior without running full mdbook builds and browser tests.

title: Technical debt: Duplicated code across 5 JavaScript backend implementations
description: There are 5 separate JS implementations (4336 total lines) with significant code duplication: comments.js (719 lines), comments-json-server.js (751 lines), comments-neon.js (988 lines), comments-supabase.js (804 lines), comments-googlesheets.js (1074 lines). Much of the UI rendering, fuzzy matching, DOM manipulation, and event handling is duplicated across all files. Should refactor to: (1) Extract common UI/matching logic into a shared module, (2) Create thin backend adapters that only handle API calls, (3) Use composition instead of duplication.

title: Technical debt: Asset injection bloats HTML by duplicating JS/CSS in every chapter
description: Currently CSS and JS are embedded inline in every chapter's HTML. For a book with N chapters, we duplicate the entire JavaScript (~1000 lines) and CSS N times. This bloats HTML files and prevents effective browser caching. Should instead: (1) Output JS/CSS as separate files in book output directory, (2) Inject <script src="..."  and <link rel="stylesheet"...> tags instead of inline code, or (3) Only inject into index.html and use shared layout. This would reduce HTML size significantly and improve caching.

title: Documentation: Missing instructions for selecting/configuring backend

Need to either: (1) Document the expected configuration if it exists, or (2) Add the configuration mechanism if it doesn't exist, or (3) Document that users need to manually swap JS files (current workaround).

title: Investigate: Could we use mdbook's additional-js/additional-css with dynamically written files?

Alternative approach: Write CSS/JS files to book's src directory during preprocessing, add them to book config's additional-js/additional-css arrays, then clean up after build. This would: (1) Keep single binary, (2) Let mdbook handle asset inclusion in all pages, (3) Enable browser caching. Trade-offs: (1) More complex, (2) Must handle cleanup, (3) Thread safety if multiple builds run. Worth investigating if it's cleaner than current inline approach.

title: Consider migrating frontend from vanilla JS to React or modern framework

title: Add unit tests for textSimilarity() Jaccard similarity function
description:
The textSimilarity() function (base.tsx:~275) implements Jaccard similarity for fuzzy text matching. This is core to comment-to-paragraph matching and needs thorough testing.

Current algorithm:
- Tokenizes both input texts
- Calculates intersection and union of token sets
- Returns intersection_size / union_size (Jaccard coefficient)

Test cases needed:
1. Identical texts: similarity = 1.0
2. Completely different texts: similarity = 0.0  
3. Partial overlap: 'hello world' vs 'hello universe' → 0.33
4. Subset relationship: 'hello' vs 'hello world' → 0.5
5. Different word order: 'hello world' vs 'world hello' → 1.0
6. Case differences: 'Hello World' vs 'hello world' → 1.0
7. Empty strings: '', 'text' → 0.0
8. Both empty: '', '' → handle gracefully
9. Punctuation differences: 'Hello, world!' vs 'Hello world' → 1.0
10. Real paragraph examples with similarity thresholds

This directly affects whether comments match correctly to moved paragraphs.

title: Add unit tests for arraySimilarity() heading path matching
description:
The arraySimilarity() function (base.tsx:~285) calculates similarity between heading paths for comment matching. Critical for maintaining comments when headings change.

Current algorithm:  
- Compares two arrays of heading strings
- Uses textSimilarity() for each pair
- Returns average similarity across all pairs
- Handles different array lengths

Test cases needed:
1. Identical arrays: ['Chapter 1', 'Section A'] vs ['Chapter 1', 'Section A'] → 1.0
2. Different lengths: ['Ch 1'] vs ['Ch 1', 'Sec A'] → test boundary handling
3. Partial matches: ['Introduction'] vs ['Intro'] → test text similarity propagation
4. Completely different: ['Chapter 1'] vs ['Appendix A'] → low similarity
5. Empty arrays: [], ['heading'] → 0.0  
6. Both empty: [], [] → handle gracefully
7. Reordered headings: ['A', 'B'] vs ['B', 'A'] → test position sensitivity
8. Case/punctuation: ['Chapter 1: Introduction'] vs ['chapter 1 introduction'] → high similarity
9. Real-world heading changes: ['Getting Started'] vs ['Quick Start Guide']

This affects comment matching when heading hierarchies are restructured.

title: Add unit tests for calculateSimilarity() core matching algorithm

Current algorithm:
- Compares comment content vs paragraph content (text similarity)
- Compares comment heading path vs paragraph heading path (array similarity)  
- Weights both factors to compute final similarity score
- Used to determine if comments should be matched to moved/edited paragraphs

Test cases needed:
1. Perfect match: identical content + identical headings → 1.0
2. Content-only match: same content, different headings → test weighting
3. Heading-only match: different content, same headings → test weighting  
4. Partial content match: edited paragraph content → test threshold behavior
5. Moved paragraph: same content, different heading path → test heading weight
6. No match: completely different content + headings → ~0.0
7. Edge cases: empty content, empty headings
8. Real-world scenarios: paragraph with minor edits + heading changes
9. Boundary testing around similarity_threshold (0.85 default)
10. Weighting validation: ensure content vs heading balance is appropriate

This function determines whether users keep their comments when content moves/changes.

title: Add unit tests for matchComments() two-pass matching algorithm
description:

Current algorithm:
- Pass 1: Exact matching (comment.paragraph_id === paragraph.id)
- Pass 2: Fuzzy matching using calculateSimilarity() for unmatched comments
- Tracks matched/unmatched comments and paragraphs
- Handles orphaned comments that can't be matched

Test cases needed:
1. Perfect scenario: all comments have exact paragraph_id matches
2. Mixed scenario: some exact matches, some need fuzzy matching
3. Moved paragraphs: comments match via fuzzy logic after content moves
4. Orphaned comments: comments that can't match any current paragraph
5. Multiple candidates: comment could match multiple paragraphs (highest similarity wins)
6. Similarity threshold: comments below threshold become orphaned  
7. Empty inputs: no comments, no paragraphs, one empty
8. Duplicate paragraph IDs: edge case handling
9. Performance: large numbers of comments and paragraphs
10. Real workflow: comment survives through paragraph edits and moves

This function determines the overall success of comment persistence across document changes.

title: Add unit tests for buildReplyStructure() nested comment tree builder

2. Nested replies: parent → reply → reply-to-reply chains
3. Multiple reply threads: several independent reply chains
4. Orphaned replies: replies with invalid parent_id
5. Circular references: reply that somehow references itself/ancestor
6. Out-of-order data: child comment appears before parent in array
7. Mixed depths: some comments with deep nesting, some standalone
8. Empty input: no comments, empty array

title: conf: Support per-tool config files with native schemas
description:
Allow users to manage each tool's config in separate files using the tool's native schema format, instead of the current centralized ~/.config/conf/config.toml structure.

## Current approach (centralized)
```toml
[tools.jj]
name = 'jj'
config_path = '~/.config/jj/config.toml'
schema_path = 'embedded://jj.json'

[tools.jj.values]
'user.email' = 'emily@artyom.me'
'user.name' = 'Emily'
```

## Proposed approach (per-tool files)
File: ~/.config/conf/jj.toml
```toml
# Native jj schema - same format as ~/.config/jj/config.toml!
user.email = 'emily@artyom.me'
user.name = 'Emily'

# Conf metadata under special key
_conf.enabled = true
_conf.config_path = '~/.config/jj/config.toml'
```

## Benefits
- Native schema format (users can copy/paste from tool docs)
- No nested structure (tools.jj.values)
- Each tool's config is self-contained
- Easier to understand and edit

## Design considerations
- Metadata key: Could be "$conf", "_conf", "_", or similar
- Multiple configs per file: Out of scope - TOML limitations:
  - No multiple documents (unlike YAML's ---)
  - No top-level arrays
  - Would need different format (YAML? JSON?)

## Implementation approach
- One file per tool: ~/.config/conf/{tool}.toml
- Load and merge all tool configs
- Validate against tool's native schema
- Backward compatibility with current config.toml format

This is a significant refactor but would make conf much more intuitive.
notes: NO BACKWARDS COMPATIBILITY NEEDED - no users yet. See mono-447 for schema validation research.

title: conf: Research metadata storage that doesn't break schema validation
description:
When using per-tool config files with native schemas, we need a way to store conf metadata without breaking schema validators.

## Problem
If ~/.config/conf/jj.toml uses jj's native schema:
```toml
user.email = 'emily@artyom.me'
user.name = 'Emily'

_conf.enabled = true  # ❌ Schema validator will complain!
```

VSCode/editors with schema validation will flag `_conf` as unknown because jj's schema doesn't include it.

## Research needed
1. **Separate metadata file**
   - ~/.config/conf/jj.toml (pure jj config)
   - ~/.config/conf/jj.meta.toml (conf metadata)
   - Pros: Clean separation, no schema issues
   - Cons: Two files per tool

2. **Comments with structured data**
   - Use TOML comments with special syntax
   - Parse comments for metadata
   - Pros: Single file
   - Cons: Hacky, fragile

3. **Schema extension**
   - Extend jj schema to include _conf
   - Pros: Proper validation
   - Cons: Need to maintain extended schemas

4. **Ignore validation errors**
   - Use additionalProperties or similar
   - Let users ignore the warnings
   - Pros: Simple
   - Cons: Annoying warnings

5. **No metadata in config files**
   - Store metadata elsewhere (database, separate file)
   - Config files are pure tool configs
   - Pros: Cleanest
   - Cons: Where to store metadata?

## Decision criteria
- Minimal user friction
- Works with existing tooling (VSCode, etc.)
- Easy to implement and maintain
- Clear mental model

Deliverable: Design document with recommendation
design:
# Metadata Storage Research

## Analysis of Options

### Option 1: Separate metadata file ⭐ RECOMMENDED
**Structure:**
```
~/.config/conf/config.toml     # Metadata for all tools
~/.config/conf/jj.toml          # Pure jj values
~/.config/conf/mise.toml        # Pure mise values
```

**config.toml content:**
```toml
[tools.jj]
name = 'jj'
config_path = '~/.config/jj/config.toml'
schema_path = 'embedded://jj.json'

[tools.mise]
name = 'mise'
config_path = '~/.config/mise/config.toml'
schema_path = 'embedded://mise.toml'
```

**jj.toml content (pure jj schema):**
```toml
user.name = 'Emily'
user.email = 'emily@artyom.me'
```

**Pros:**
- No schema validation issues
- Clean separation: metadata vs values
- Single metadata file for all tools
- Per-tool value files use native schemas
- Easy to understand and maintain

**Cons:**
- Still have config.toml (not fully per-tool)
- Need to load two files per tool

### Option 2: Metadata in comments
**Example:**
```toml
# _conf: {"config_path": "~/.config/jj/config.toml"}
user.name = 'Emily'
```

**Pros:** Single file
**Cons:** Hacky, fragile, loses comments on save

### Option 3: Schema extension
**Pros:** Proper validation
**Cons:** Maintenance burden, need to update with upstream changes

### Option 4: Ignore validation errors
**Pros:** Simple
**Cons:** Poor UX, confusing warnings

### Option 5: Database for metadata
**Pros:** Clean separation
**Cons:** Added complexity, not human-editable

## Recommendation

**Use Option 1 (Separate metadata file)**

The key insight is that conf needs TWO types of data:
1. **Metadata**: Where files are, what schemas to use (conf-specific)
2. **Values**: Actual config values (tool-specific)

Keep metadata in config.toml, move values to per-tool files.

## Implementation Plan

1. Keep ~/.config/conf/config.toml for tool metadata
2. Add ~/.config/conf/{tool}.toml for tool values (optional)
3. When loading: merge metadata from config.toml with values from {tool}.toml
4. When saving values: write to {tool}.toml if it exists, else to config.toml

## Migration Path

Existing config works as-is (values in config.toml).
New style: create separate jj.toml and remove [tools.jj.values] section.
Gradual migration - both formats coexist.

title: conf: Implement iCloud Drive sync for config files
description:
Add a `conf sync` command that uses iCloud Drive as a bidirectional sync mechanism for configuration files across machines.

## Design philosophy
- Keep files in ~/.config (normal locations)
- Use iCloud Drive as sync intermediary, NOT as primary storage
- Bidirectional: push local changes, pull remote changes
- Selective: sync only what user wants

## Use case
Alice has 3 machines:
1. Work laptop - has jj config
2. Home desktop - has jj + mise config  
3. iPad - wants to view/edit configs

With `conf sync`:
```bash
# On work laptop
conf sync push    # Push jj config to iCloud Drive

# On home desktop
conf sync pull    # Get jj config from iCloud
conf sync push    # Push both jj + mise to iCloud

# Result: All machines have jj, home has mise
```

## Key design questions to explore

### 1. Sync strategy
- Full sync vs selective (per-tool)?
- Conflict resolution (last-write-wins? merge? manual?)
- Tracking: How to know what changed?

### 2. Storage structure in iCloud
```
~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/conf/
  jj.toml
  mise.toml
  .sync-metadata/
    jj.json      # timestamps, checksums?
    mise.json
```

### 3. Commands
```bash
conf sync push [tool]      # Push to iCloud
conf sync pull [tool]      # Pull from iCloud
conf sync status          # Show what's different
conf sync diff [tool]     # Show actual differences
conf sync resolve [tool]  # Handle conflicts
```

### 4. Metadata tracking
- Last sync time per tool
- Machine identification (hostname?)
- Conflict detection
- Change detection (hash? mtime?)

### 5. Edge cases
- No iCloud Drive (should fail gracefully)
- Multiple machines pushing simultaneously
- Partial sync failures
- Corrupted sync data
- First-time sync (no existing iCloud data)

## Technical considerations
- iCloud Drive path: ~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/
- Change detection: File hashes vs mtimes
- Locking: Prevent concurrent writes
- Backup: Before overwriting local files
- Dry-run mode: Preview changes

## Future enhancements (out of scope for v1)
- Auto-sync on config change
- Sync to other backends (Dropbox, Google Drive, S3)
- Selective key sync (not whole files)
- Encrypted sync
- Git-based sync

## Dependencies
- Requires per-tool config file structure (mono-446)
- Should work with any sync backend, iCloud just first impl

This needs careful design before implementation.

title: conf: Implement simple merge-based iCloud sync (MVP)
description:
Simpler sync implementation than the full bidirectional sync (mono-448). Just download, merge, upload.

## Algorithm (simple)
```
1. Download config from iCloud Drive
2. Merge with local config (union of keys)
3. Upload merged result back to iCloud
4. Done
```

## Not trying to be smart
- No conflict resolution UI
- No "which machine last changed what"
- No selective sync
- Just merge everything together

## Key question: Conflict detection
When do we know there's a real conflict vs. just different keys?

**Options:**
1. **eTag** (HTTP-style)
   - Store hash of last known iCloud state
   - Before merge, check if iCloud changed
   - If changed, someone else modified it
   
2. **Vector clocks**
   - Each machine has a counter
   - Track which machine made which change
   - Can detect concurrent modifications
   
3. **Last-Write-Wins (LWW) timestamps**
   - Store timestamp with each key
   - Newer timestamp wins
   - Simple but can lose data
   
4. **No conflict detection**
   - Just merge (union)
   - If same key has different values, pick one (local? remote?)
   - Simplest but dangerous

## Example merge behavior
```
Local:
  user.name = "Emily"
  user.email = "emily@artyom.me"
  
iCloud:
  user.name = "Emily April"
  ui.editor = "vim"

Merged result (uploaded back):
  user.name = ??? # Conflict! Which one?
  user.email = "emily@artyom.me"
  ui.editor = "vim"
```

## Proposed MVP approach
1. **Hash-based change detection**
   - Store SHA256 of iCloud version we last saw
   - Before merge: check if iCloud hash changed
   - If unchanged: safe to upload our changes
   - If changed: do merge with LWW on conflicts

2. **Last-Write-Wins on conflicts**
   - For same key with different values: take most recent
   - Store mtime for each key? Or file-level?
   - File-level is simpler: compare file mtimes

3. **Metadata file**
   ```
   ~/.config/conf/.sync-state
   jj:
     last_icloud_hash: "abc123..."
     last_sync_time: "2025-10-22T18:00:00Z"
   ```

## Commands
```bash
conf sync           # Do the merge sync
conf sync --dry-run # Show what would happen
conf sync status    # Show last sync info
```

## Edge cases
- First sync (no iCloud data): upload local
- First sync (no local data): download from iCloud
- Simultaneous syncs from different machines: LWW wins
- Deleted keys: Hard to detect - ignore for MVP

## What this doesn't do (vs mono-448)
- No push/pull separation
- No selective sync
- No real conflict resolution UI
- No change tracking beyond hash
- No sync history

This is the dumb version that just works for simple cases.

title: conf: Preserve comments and formatting in per-tool config files
description:
Currently, when conf modifies per-tool config files (e.g., ~/.config/conf/jj.toml), it performs a full rewrite using toml.Marshal(). This destroys:
- Comments added by users
- Custom formatting/whitespace
- Original path notation (~ vs /Users/)

## Current Behavior
User creates jj.toml with comments:
```toml
# My jj configuration
[user]
name = 'John'  # Full name
```

After running `conf jj user.email "john@example.com"`, comments are lost:
```toml
[user]
email = 'john@example.com'
name = 'John'
```

## Desired Behavior
Surgical edits that preserve all existing content and only modify the specific value being changed.

## Research Done
- go-toml v2 explicitly does NOT support comment preservation (out of scope)
- No Go libraries exist for comment-preserving TOML editing
- Rust's toml_edit crate does this well
- YAML has go-yaml v3 with yaml.Node for this

## Possible Solutions
1. Build custom line-based surgical editor (simple cases only)
2. Shell out to Rust toml CLI tool (external dependency)
3. Port toml_edit approach to Go (significant effort)
4. Accept limitation and document it (current choice)

## Current Status
Documented as known limitation. Users should avoid adding important comments to files managed by conf, or accept that they will be reformatted.

2. Add safeguards to prevent writing test-like values in production
3. Add validation to ensure test isolation is maintained
4. Implement better separation between test and production code
